I'm sure a lot of you are aware of these, and what they do, but I'm going to dumb it down a tad for anyone who happens to stumble across this post.

 

GIMP :Image editor.

A metric shit-ton of features. A little daunting if you're new to it, but lots of good tutorials online, and like a lot of software you're not going to use most of the features, so don't be intimidated by all the buttons. I highly recommend the G'MIC plugin.

Rawtherapee :Image processing.

I'm just now getting to know this one so I can't really comment on it so far. I do know it automates a lot of post processing tasks and handles batch commands. Someone with more experience should chime in on this, as I don't really know enough about it.

Inkscape :Vector graphics.

A little buggy, will crash on you sometimes, but it does a damn good job when it comes to vectors. If you use GIMP, and need a better text solution, this is it. Can copy and paste images from GIMP without saving them. Way more than a glorified text creator though. This guy concentrates on logos, but his tutorials are the best I've found so far for learning Inkscape. Short, sweet, and to the point. Also has some decent GIMP tutorials.

Krita :Drawing.

I can't draw worth a shit, but I love playing around with this. I even bought a drawing pad for it. Does handle vector and polygon, but not as well as dedicated software. Import an image to a layer, and get your trace on.

Shoutcut :Video editing.

I'm sure there's better out there, but this is the one I'm familiar with. Splicing, fades, simple tasks like that are just a matter of drag and drop. Lots of filters and features. Does chroma key (green screen) and is now my go-to for gif creation. Made this gif using Shotcut and GIMP.

Blender :3d modeling and rendering, but does a lot of shit including video editing.

To me this is the best piece of free/open source software out there. It does amazing shit. This isn't a pic, but was modeled in Blender. Seriously steep learning curve, but this guy's free tutorials will get you up and running in no time. Fair warning though, like all rendering software this bitch eats memory. The main problem with GIMP (vs photoshop) right now is that gimp doesn't have "non destructive editing." What that basically means is that e.g. in photoshop, you can add some text, apply some filters to it, and then afterwards you can change the text and the filters are reapplied to the new text. Everything in the background is unaffected. Basically ps keeps a stack of operations to apply instead of (almost) always doing a single job directly to the layer. In GIMP, you add some text, and if you want to change it you can do it now, but only now, before applying filters and such. That is unless you want to redo your work manually (which you can, of course, if you keep the text in its own layer and remember everything you applied to it.) It would be a really massive undertaking to add that to GIMP but it'd be very convenient to have. Also since ps is designed this way there are probably things you "just can't do" without it, but I wouldn't really know since I've happily used GIMP for 20 years or some shit
